Standing orders are the procedural rules of parliament. The motion had been introduced by Liberal MP Alan Tudge (for Aston). ### Motion text > *That so much of the standing orders be suspended as would prevent the motion for the third reading being moved without delay.* ### What is this bill all about? The [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5866) was introduced to implement the Coalition Government's new school funding proposal. Unfortunately, at the time of this vote there was still no bills digest to explain exactly what the new proposal is, but there is a [very helpful and easy to understand explanation on The Conversation](http://theconversation.com/confused-about-changes-to-school-funding-heres-what-you-need-to-know-78455) by Associate Professor Misty Adoniou. As a brief summary: * the proposal offers more money for schools, but less than the previous Labor Government had offered; * every student will attract the same amount of funding but the amount of funding that the federal government will provide (as opposed to the state governments) is not equal between government and non-government schools (that is, the federal government will provide 80% of the funding for non-government schools but only 20% for government schools, with the states paying the difference); * those in need will get more funding, but the Government still doesn't have any proposal for how this will work or even how many students will be eligible for this, which leaves a big question mark over the whole proposal. ### How are schools currently fun

The speaker opposed the Australian Education Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would cut $22.3 billion from schools, with an average loss of $2.4 million per school, and disproportionately harm public schools while wealthy private schools gain funding. Specific examples included $846 million lost by New South Wales public schools over two years and $19 million gained by The King's School in Sydney.

The member opposed the Australian Education Amendment Bill 2017, calling it a betrayal of needs-based Gonski funding and citing a $22 billion overall cut, $630 million removed from Victorian public schools over two years, and $65 billion in company tax cuts prioritised over education. They also criticised the bill's lack of transparency, weak state funding commitments, and named affected schools including Mill Park Secondary College ($1.8 million cut), Epping Secondary College, and Epping Views Primary School ($800,000 cut).

The Australian Education Amendment Bill 2017 would deepen inequities between students and schools, boost inequality generally, and represent a retreat from national responsibility for education. The bill was rejected on the grounds that every child deserves every chance to fulfil their potential.

The speaker argued in support of the Australian Education Amendment Bill 2017, which implements the coalition's Quality Schools package with $242.3 billion in total schools recurrent funding from 2018 to 2027, including $81.1 billion from 2018 to 2021. The bill establishes needs-based funding, removes 27 secret deals from Labor, and ties funding to reforms, with specific mention of The Glenleighden School in Ryan and 18 other local schools.

The speaker criticised Labor for failing to implement the original Gonski review and noted that two schools in the electorate—Mount St Benedict College and Oakhill College—would receive less funding under the new arrangements.

This bill would overhaul how the Australian Human Rights Commission handles discrimination complaints.
It would require the commission to treat both sides fairly and to throw out weak complaints early.
The changes implement most of a parliamentary committee's recommendations from a February 2017 report on free speech.
The bill would set new rules for lodging, investigating and referring discrimination complaints to court.
It would make the commission notify people accused of discrimination when a complaint is lodged.
It would remove unmeritorious claims at the outset and speed up the process.
The bill would also cut red tape for the commission by easing reporting duties and clarifying its mediation procedures.
Anyone who makes or faces a complaint of unlawful discrimination, as well as the Australian Human Rights Commission itself.

The bill would stop modern awards from being changed to reduce employees' take-home pay, including cuts to penalty rates or the hours they apply to.
It would amend the Fair Work Act 2009 to prevent the Fair Work Commission from varying a modern award if the change would likely reduce any employee's take-home pay.
The bill would also invalidate any determination from the Fair Work Commission's decision AM2014/305 that would cut take-home pay, and it would take effect the day after Royal Assent.

Defines take-home pay to include wages, incentive payments, allowances, and overtime, and ensures employees receive the full benefit of minimum wage increases.
Employees covered by modern awards, including prospective employees, and the Fair Work Commission.

The changes apply to agreements registered or lodged for registration on or before 2 February 2017.
It validates existing area agreements that were registered before the court decision but did not have all signatures.
It allows registration of agreements that were lodged before the court decision but lack all signatures.
It clarifies who must be a party to future area agreements unless the claim group chooses otherwise.
Native title holders, parties to area Indigenous Land Use Agreements, and the native title sector.

The majority voted in favour of an [amendment](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-05-11.167.1) introduced by Labor Party Senator [Malarndirri McCarthy](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/nt/malarndirri_mccarthy) (NT), which means the amendment was successful. ### What was the amendment? The amendment didn't change the bill at all, it just added words to the motion of [whether to agree with the bill's main idea](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/divisions/senate/2017-06-13/6). In parliamentary jargon, it added the words below to the motion that the bill be [read for a second time](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ### Wording of the amendment > *At the end of the motion [to read the bill for a second time], add:* > *but the Senate expresses its disappointment with the regrettable way in which the Government has managed the process for consultation on the changes contained in the Bill, which has been a source of unnecessary angst, confusion and delay."* ### What is this bill all about? The bill is [a response](http://www.indigenous.gov.au/news-and-media/announcements/nttt-government-introduces-legislation-address-mcglade-decision) to [McGlade v Native Title Registrar & Ors [2017] FCAFC 10](http://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/sinodisp/au/cases/cth/FCAFC/2017/10.html?query=), which considers whether an Indigenous Land Use Agreement (**ILUA**) can be registered with the Native Title Registrar even if not all named parties have signed. An Indigenous Land Use Agreement is a voluntary agreement that native title groups can negotiate with other parties in relation to the use of land and waters. In that case, the Federal Court ruled that all parties must sign, which meant the Noongar Native Title agreement could not be registered (read more in [ABC News](http://www.abc.net.au/news/2017-02-02/billon-dollar-noongar-native-title-deal-rejected-by-court/8235138)). The bill restores the pre-McGlade legal position so that Indigenous land use agreements are valid if authorised by the broader native title claim group, even if not all registered native title claimants sign, and applies retrospectively to protect existing and pending agreements.

The opposition criticized the government for rushing debate on the Native Title Amendment (Indigenous Land Use Agreements) Bill 2017 only 24 hours after its introduction, arguing it stemmed from Attorney-General George Brandis's incompetence in failing to act on warnings about the full Federal Court's McGlade decision (2 February 2017) which could invalidate around 150 existing Indigenous land use agreements. The opposition accepted the need for the bill but condemned the lack of consultation with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities and stakeholders, and noted the government's failure to respond to the 2015 Australian Law Reform Commission report on native title.

The Native Title Amendment (Indigenous Land Use Agreements) Bill 2017 responds to the Federal Court's McGlade decision by removing the requirement for all registered native title claimants to sign an Indigenous Land Use Agreement, restoring the previous status quo; the government intends to pass the bill through the House and consult for four weeks before Senate consideration, noting 123 existing agreements are affected, 109 in Queensland.

The Labor Party argued the Native Title Amendment Bill 2017 was rushed without consultation, criticising the Attorney-General for disrespecting Indigenous communities and failing to prepare for a Federal Court ruling that invalidated 123 Indigenous Land Use Agreements. Labor stated it would protect native title but would not support legislation introduced with only a day's notice.

The speaker argued that the Native Title Amendment (Indigenous Land Use Agreements) Bill 2017 is necessary to remedy uncertainty caused by the February 2017 McGlade v Native Title Registrar Federal Court decision, which invalidated area ILUAs not signed by all registered native title claimants. The bill would secure existing agreements, enable registration of lodged agreements, and clarify future party requirements, with the speaker urging all parties to support the amendments to provide certainty for Indigenous communities and economic opportunities.

The Native Title Amendment (Indigenous Land Use Agreements) Bill 2017 was rushed into the House despite the Attorney-General, Senator Brandis, having been warned months earlier—including via a leaked August letter from Indigenous groups—that urgent technical amendments were needed to prevent a Federal Court decision invalidating land-use agreements across Australia.
Labor agreed to a gag on the Native Title Amendment (Indigenous Land Use Agreements) Bill, pushing it through without proper scrutiny despite a list of speakers opposing the fast-tracked passage.

The Native Title Amendment (Indigenous Land Use Agreements) Bill is urgent and merely restores the status quo understood before the Federal Court’s 2 February decision, with no significant stakeholder opposition.

The government was condemned for rushing the Native Title Amendment (Indigenous Land Use Agreements) Bill 2017 through Parliament with only a five-minute second reading speech and no consultation, contradicting the Prime Minister’s stated commitment to partnership with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

The Native Title Amendment (Indigenous Land Use Agreements) Bill 2017 passed the Senate with two sets of government amendments: one removing measures not required to address the McGlade decision, and another protecting Indigenous land use agreements in Cape York at the request of the Cape York Land Council. The bill aims to provide certainty for existing and future ILUAs and maintain them as a key mechanism for Indigenous Australians to enjoy social and economic benefits from native title rights.

Labor supported the amended bill after securing changes through a Senate committee, including preventing the government from taking unfettered control over Indigenous land use agreements and ensuring consultation with communities like the Cape York Land Council. The opposition criticised the government for originally attempting to rush the bill without proper consultation, citing the need to validate 126 land use agreements affected by the February 2 McGlade Federal Court decision.

The speaker opposed the bill, arguing the PaTH program would create a pool of cheap labour for businesses, potentially displacing jobs, undercutting wages, and compromising participant safety, and moved an amendment demanding the government guarantee against job displacement, wage undercutting, safety risks, sidestepping of unfair dismissal protections, and prioritisation of small to medium enterprises.

The speaker argued that the Youth Jobs PaTH program will prepare unemployed young Australians for real workplaces through internships, training and wage subsidies, citing 600,000 people in jobless households as a key concern. He linked job creation to free trade agreements with China, Japan and South Korea, and referenced local examples like nectarine exports to China and table grapes to support the claim that market access is generating employment opportunities.

The speaker argued that the PaTH program in the bill is poorly designed, likely to exploit young jobseekers with below-award wages and internships that don't lead to jobs, and cited criticisms from ACOSS, the ACTU, NUS, and the Institute of Public Affairs. They noted youth unemployment rates of 12.8% nationally, nearly 20% in southeast Melbourne, and over 30% in some migrant communities in their electorate of Bruce.

The speaker argued that the Youth Jobs PaTH program will break cycles of intergenerational welfare dependency by providing employability training, paid work experience ($200 per fortnight on top of welfare), and employer incentives, targeting 120,000 young people over four years. The bill ensures participants' extra payments do not affect other entitlements and allows easy return to income support if a job ends through no fault of their own.

The opposition criticised the PaTH program as a hastily cobbled-together scheme that could exploit young jobseekers with below-award wages and inadequate workers' compensation, citing youth unemployment at 12.8% (271,400 aged 15–24) and 170,900 underemployed; they called for a Senate inquiry and noted that 90% of Work for the Dole participants do not gain full-time work.

The bill establishes the Youth Jobs PaTH program, investing $751.7 million over four years to provide pre-employment training, paid internships, and wage subsidies for jobseekers under 25, alongside additional measures like the Youth Bonus wage subsidy and expanded New Enterprise Incentive Scheme.

The speech called for the Youth Jobs PaTH bill to be referred to a Senate inquiry, arguing the program could lead to exploitation of young workers, undermine wages, and displace existing employees, and noting that 90% of Work for the Dole participants did not find full-time work after the program.

The speaker argued for the Youth Jobs PaTH program, which includes employability skills training, voluntary internships with a $200 fortnightly payment to participants, and wage subsidies of $6,500–$10,000 for employers hiring young jobseekers, with up to 120,000 placements over four years. The bill ensures internship payments are not counted as income for social security purposes.

The speaker argued that the Youth Jobs PaTH program will help young jobseekers avoid long-term welfare dependency by providing practical work experience, using the Bunbury Senior High School's Shed Works program in Western Australia as a successful example. The speaker cited the $200 fortnightly incentive for interns and provisions to protect social security payments, and urged support for the 2016 bill.

The speaker opposed the 2016 Youth Jobs Path bill, arguing it is not a jobs plan but an exploitation program that lacks safeguards, depresses wages, and displaces existing jobs, citing examples such as $4‑per‑hour supermarket internships and wage subsidies for companies like Coles and Safeway that already hire young people.
